It supports dual SIM through nano-SIM and eSIM, as well as dual eSIM.- Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Features Privacy Display, Samsung Knox Vault, KEEP and Knox Matrix security technologies. Its Quick Share feature also supports sharing with compatible Apple devices through AirDrop compatibility, according to the supplied specifications.

title: REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ launched with 185Hz display, RGB water cooling and 8,400mAh battery: check prices and top features
title_bn: REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ launched with 185Hz display, RGB water cooling and 8,400mAh battery: check prices and top features
author: TechPulse
excerpt: REDMAGIC has launched the 12 Pro+ in China, starting at 6,999 yuan. The gaming phone features a 185Hz under-display-camera screen, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, 8,400mAh battery, and combined air and liquid cooling.
paragraph1: REDMAGIC has launched the 12 Pro+ in China, starting at 6,999 yuan. The gaming phone features a 185Hz under-display-camera screen, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, 8,400mAh battery, and combined air and liquid cooling.REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ launched with 185Hz display: check prices and top features (Image: X)REDMAGIC has brought its latest high-end gaming smartphone, the REDMAGIC 12 Pro+, to the Chinese market, with the base variant priced at 6,999 yuan (around ₹99,395).The new model features a see-through mechanical-style exterior, a 185Hz screen and a combination of air and liquid cooling technology. It also houses an 8,400mAh battery, according to Fone Arena. Alongside the standard variants, the company has announced a Golden Saga special edition with 24GB RAM and 1TB internal storage.The phone follows REDMAGIC's signature industrial design, with a transparent rear cover and a flat body intended to make landscape-oriented gaming more comfortable. Its back panel showcases a two-ring liquid-cooling arrangement, with an RGB illuminated circle positioned at the centre.Buyers have been given options to choose from Deuterium Transparent Night, Deuterium Transparent Silver Wing and Deuterium Transparent Ice Blue colour options.Battery, software and pricingThe smartphone is 8.55mm thick and weighs 223 grams.
paragraph2: Its 8,400mAh battery supports wired charging at up to 120W and wireless charging at up to 80W. A bypass charging option is also available, allowing power to be supplied directly during gaming to help limit heat build-up.On the software front, the device runs Android 17 with REDMAGIC OS 12. The interface includes the Magic Island notification feature, an upgraded AI assistant, tools for writing and transcription, and a file-sharing feature that enables transfers between the phone and Apple iOS devices. Its gaming suite offers peripheral controls and wireless screen casting at resolutions of up to 8K at 60Hz or 4K at 144Hz.In China, the REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is priced as follows:12GB RAM and 256GB storage: 6,999 yuan (approximately ₹99,395)16GB RAM and 512GB storage: 7,999 yuan (approximately ₹1,13,595)16GB RAM and 1TB storage: 8,999 yuan (approximately ₹1,27,795)The Golden Saga Limited Edition, equipped with 24GB RAM and 1TB storage, will be introduced at a later date. The standard REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is already available for purchase in China.For its international launch, REDMAGIC plans to market the handset under the name REDMAGIC 12 Pro. Details covering overseas prices, configurations and market availability are expected to be announced on November 3 this year.185Hz display and gaming capabilitiesREDMAGIC has worked with BOE on the phone's front panel, which uses ninth-generation under-display camera technology to achieve an uninterrupted screen design. The OLED display has extremely narrow 0.
paragraph3: 96mm borders and offers a refresh rate of up to 185Hz, while also supporting 165Hz operation. A dedicated G1 display processor, produced using a 22nm manufacturing process, works with X11 luminescent material.For touch input, the smartphone uses a Synaptics Byrd controller and the MagicTouch 4.0 algorithm. According to the company, touch sampling reaches 500Hz across the screen and can peak at 5,000Hz in instantaneous measurements. The panel also incorporates SGS-certified Star Shield Eye Protection Technology 2.0. For front-facing photography and video calls, the device has a 16MP camera concealed beneath the display.Processor and cooling technologyThe REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, built on TSMC's 2nm technology and capable of reaching clock speeds of 5GHz. The processor works alongside REDMAGIC's in-house Red Core R5 chip, which takes care of tasks including touch response optimisation, lighting control, frame tracking and display upscaling.The company says the handset scored 5,670,006 points on AnTuTu and delivers a 44% gain in GPU performance.
paragraph4:
It also brings full-scene ray tracing to six games at launch. Among the supported gaming features are 185Hz gameplay for CrossFire: Mobile and simultaneous 2K resolution and 185Hz enhancements in 10 titles.To control temperatures during demanding workloads, REDMAGIC has equipped the phone with its ICE Magic Cooling System. The setup combines a mechanical fan with a Liquid-cooling circuit.Its Wind Chaser 5.0 fan operates at speeds of up to 25,500rpm, while a dual-crystal micro-pump pushes dielectric fluid through the cooling loop. The thermal assembly is further supported by Liquid Metal 4.0, a vapour chamber and graphene-based layers.About the AuthorGarvit BhiraniGarvit Bhirani is a journalist based in Gurugram. He is a Deputy Chief Content Producer at LiveMint, where he covers national and international news stories, focusing on accuracy and compelling storytelling for readers.

With a total of six years of experience in journalism, he has previously worked with Vaco Binary Semantics for Google, taking on the role of news curation lead, and reported from the field on health, education, and agriculture stories for 101reporters and News9.
paragraph5:
He has also served as a content editor for entertainment and news media organisations.

Garvit holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in journalism and mass communication from Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University and Gurugram University, respectively. During college days, he joined India’s only non-profit student journalism network, where he anchored daily news updates and produced his own weekly show called ‘Data Fix’.

He was selected for the YES Foundation Media for Social Change Fellowship in Delhi, the Talking Data to the Fourth Pillar residential workshop, and the VOICE Fellowship in Pune.

He holds certificates in COVID-19-verification reporting, data journalism, food & agriculture, tech policy, media literacy and countering misinformation, and tackling election disinformation courses from Thomson Foundation, IndiaSpend, The Dialogue, US Mission in India, and AFP.

He can be reached on LinkedIn or on

title: Apple iPhone Duo's ‘extraordinary’ pre-order frenzy raises stakes for its foldable smartphone debut
title_bn: Apple iPhone Duo's ‘extraordinary’ pre-order frenzy raises stakes for its foldable smartphone debut
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The coming weeks will offer a clearer indication of whether the initial pre-order rush translates into sustained sales momentum and how quickly Apple can fulfil orders for its first foldable iPhone.
paragraph1: The coming weeks will offer a clearer indication of whether the initial pre-order rush translates into sustained sales momentum and how quickly Apple can fulfil orders for its first foldable iPhone.An advertisement for the iPhone Duo at the Apple Inc. store on Regent Street in London, UK, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026.
paragraph2: Photographer: Betty Laura Zapata/Bloomberg(Bloomberg)Apple Inc.’s first foldable smartphone has reportedly drawn an extraordinary rush of pre-orders, with delivery estimates slipping to the end of January within minutes of orders opening on Friday, raising the stakes for the company’s debut in the foldable phone market.Apple said demand for the iPhone Duo had been “nothing short of extraordinary” as customers encountered increasingly long waits for the device, which is scheduled to go on sale on October 23.“The pre-order demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary.
paragraph3: We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online,” the company said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.Customers who accessed Apple’s online store on Friday initially encountered delivery estimates stretching into November. Within minutes, the estimates moved to December and, in some cases, to the end of January, the news outlet reported.The delays reportedly affected both colour options and every storage configuration, ranging from 256 gigabytes to 2 terabytes, highlighting the strong initial response to Apple’s new device.
paragraph4: However, the company did not disclose whether customers who missed the initial pre-order window would be able to purchase the iPhone Duo in stores when it launches.iPhone Duo pre-order rush raises stakes for Apple’s foldable betThe initial rush marks a significant moment for Apple as it enters the foldable smartphone segment.The iPhone Duo is among the first major product launches under Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took over the role in September.The response to the iPhone Duo is particularly notable compared with the September launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
paragraph5: Customers who placed orders promptly for those models had a smoother experience, while securing the new foldable proved significantly more difficult, according to Bloomberg.The delivery delays, however, do not by themselves establish whether Apple is facing production constraints or whether the company had limited inventory available for the initial launch.

title: Decoding Urban Company’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Proposal
title_bn: Decoding Urban Company’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Proposal
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore…
paragraph1: SUMMARYThe proposed ₹2,500 Cr fundraise bolsters Urban Company's balance sheet and provides it with strategic flexibility, said CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal The company will deploy the capital towards growth investments, such as acquisitions that consolidate its position in an existing market or enter a new category It is also looking to expand into a new category by making residential air conditioners under its consumer appliances brand Native Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore up its war chest at a critical juncture. On one hand, Urban Company’s instant home services business, InstaHelp, is facing stiff competition. Fighting rivals Snabbit and Pronto for a slice of the market has turned out to be an expensive affair, with spending on InstaHelp contributing to Urban Company’s widening losses. At the same time, the company is looking to expand its product lineup under the Native brand by entering the residential air conditioner market. Meanwhile, its bread and butter consumer services continue to generate stable results. Urban Company’s financials reflect these pressures. The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by a ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding InstaHelp, it reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr. During the quarter, consolidated revenue from operations grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr, while total expenses increased 61.
paragraph2: 5% to ₹745.7 Cr. Consequently, the company’s consolidated net loss more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period. However, the management maintains that Urban Company can meet its profitability targets without the proposed fundraise Yet, the management has rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials. How Badly Does Urban Company Need The Cash? Urban Company has positioned the proposed ₹2,500 Cr fundraise as a means to bolster its balance sheet and provide greater flexibility to invest across its businesses. “Our ambition is to go beyond being just a home services company and eventually become the trusted home platform for Indian consumers – almost the operating system for the Indian home. So given that ambition, we want the strategic flexibility over the next few years to invest in all our areas of business,” CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal told analysts during the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call. The company also plans to deploy the capital towards growth opportunities, including acquisitions.
paragraph3: While no acquisition deals have been finalised till now, the management is evaluating opportunities that could help Urban Company consolidate its position in an existing market or enter a new category. Bhal added that the company would take an opportunistic approach to international markets and Native. However, an acquisition in InstaHelp would be “highly unlikely”. “If at all we do an M&A, it would be to add on categories that we don’t operate in today where we feel that the decision of build versus buy may be tilting in favour of buy,” he noted. Urban Company has guided for adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and ₹1,000 Cr in adjusted EBITDA profit by FY31. The management maintained that its current financial position, even without raising additional capital, is sufficient to meet these targets. However, Bhal acknowledged that the company’s existing balance sheet limits its financial flexibility, given InstaHelp’s losses. While the management maintains that the company can meet its profitability targets without additional capital, the proposed fundraise would provide it with greater room to invest in growth and respond to changing market conditions. In particular, Urban Company is facing intense competition in the emerging quick home services segment. For instance, after Urban Company disclosed that InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2, Snabbit’s founder Aayush Agarwal claimed that the startup had served 6.
paragraph4: 45 Mn orders during the period. Diving Into A New Market While it faces intense competition in the quick home services market, Urban Company is simultaneously looking to expand into a new category. Alongside approving the fundraise proposal, its board proposed exploring residential air conditioners as a new business under its consumer appliances brand Native, whose portfolio currently comprises water purifiers and smart locks. “We’ve now operated in the segment of air conditioning servicing and repair for close to 11-12 years, ever since the inception of the company. And there’s a lot of data and knowledge that we have gathered on what are the consumer pain points and what are some of the unmet needs of the consumers. Based on those data points and our own understanding of the market and the unmet needs, we have been quietly working on creating an innovative cutting-edge product,” Bhal told analysts on the call. The company is yet to disclose further details, including a commercial launch timeline. Notably, Inc42 reported last year about Urban Company’s potential foray into AC business. Bhal said the first one to two years in the new market would focus on learning and gathering customer feedback. He also noted that Urban Company’s app would be the sole distribution channel for its ACs. The CEO emphasised a “calibrated and measured” approach to capital allocation, adding that Native has a clear path to profitability that should not be affected by the new venture.
paragraph5: For context, Native’s net transaction value (NTV) grew 35.4% YoY in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 40% to ₹105 Cr. The segment remained loss-making on an adjusted EBITDA basis, reporting a loss of ₹9 Cr. However, loss as a percentage of NTV declined to 6.8% from 9% a year ago. Urban Company’s platform sees 10X as many AC servicing, repair, and installation orders as water purifier orders, giving it a larger existing customer base for AC-related services. This provides a potential channel to market Native’s ACs, although service demand does not necessarily translate into appliance sales. With InstaHelp facing stiff competition and Native preparing to enter a new product category, Urban Company is pursuing multiple growth opportunities even as its losses widen. The proposed fundraise would provide additional capital to support these plans, although the management maintains that the company can achieve its stated profitability targets without it.

title: HyperX Cloud Alpha Air Review: Open-back and budget-friendly
title_bn: HyperX Cloud Alpha Air Review: Open-back and budget-friendly
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The HyperX Cloud Alpha Air is the brand's first open-back gaming headset. It's lightweight and comfortable, and it sounds very good. But microphone pickup is low, and it doesn't seem to work with the brand's peripheral software (yet).
paragraph1: The Cloud Alpha Air is light, comfortable, and it sounds very good. It doesn't seem to work with HyperX's Ngenuity software, but you shouldn't need that to use this headset. Reasons to buy +Very comfortable and lightweight +Sturdy +Sounds good Reasons to avoid -Loud blip when you press the mute button -Extension system of wires is not ideal -Ngenuity doesn't work, at least not yet.

title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
title_bn: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
paragraph1: With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip. Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades. The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit.
paragraph2: Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click. Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate. It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either.
paragraph3: I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach. If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings. Image Credits:Ember The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills.
paragraph4: The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.) The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149. The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green. Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders.
paragraph5: It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out. The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon. title: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
title_bn: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier. Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band
paragraph1: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.Thanks for having me.
paragraph2: I’m looking forward to it.I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.
paragraph3: The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it.
paragraph4: Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.”At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity.So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network.
paragraph5: I’m less interested in the stock and more interested in just the cost structure of how this works. If I rewind my brain to being a baby blogger at Engadget 100 years ago, the FCC told all the TV networks they had to stop broadcasting on 700 MHz and we were going to run an auction.Verizon and AT&T bought big chunks of 700 MHz spectrum and that’s what 4G is built on. That’s the low-bandwidth spectrum that you’re talking about. It goes everywhere. This was a big victory that we reallocated 700 MHz, and 800 MHz was sitting right there the whole time. This is the Nextel spectrum. If it is so valuable, why wasn’t there a market for it until Elon showed up just now?It was part of this transaction. T-Mobile ended up having to sell it because the government said, “If we’re going to allow you to take out the fourth competitor, which was Sprint, then in order to enable another fourth competitor out there, we need to have you guys give up some of your low-band spectrum.”Part of the deal that T-Mobile and Sprint had with the government was that they would sell it to EchoStar. Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.They had the rights to buy.

Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.They had the rights to buy.

The transfers would expand IDBI’s insurance and investment services presence, subject to requisite approvals. paragraph5: On the financial front, Nazara posted a ₹82.5 Cr loss in Q1 FY27, with operating revenue falling 14% YoY to ₹428.8 Cr. Bluetile’s EBITDA remained flat despite 54% revenue growth amid higher user acquisition costs. Groww Gains Despite Flat Sequential Revenue Groww gained 4.34% to close the week ₹200.70 after its Q2 FY27 net profit rose 54% YoY to ₹724.7 Cr and operating revenue increased 47.4% YoY to ₹1,501.5 Cr. Sequentially, revenue was almost unchanged and profit fell 1.4% from ₹735 Cr. EBITDA slipped to ₹969 Cr from ₹971 Cr in the preceding June quarter. Growth in margin trading and commodity derivatives offset a 14.3% QoQ decline in equity derivatives revenue. The company attributed the decline in equity derivatives revenue to adjustments following the closing auction system’s (CAS) introduction. Expenses rose 28.5% YoY to ₹555.9 Cr, reflecting higher technology costs, AI-linked and other compute cost inflation, and ₹13 Cr in client reimbursements following a third-party market infrastructure institution’s operational issue. Groww AMC’s assets under management rose 145% YoY to ₹7,179 Cr, although it posted a ₹8.3 Cr quarterly loss. title: AI lab offers free plumbing and HVAC repairs across three cities to train AI robots
title_bn: AI lab offers free plumbing and HVAC repairs across three cities to train AI robots
author: TechPulse
excerpt: HUMXN wants to pay for maintenance and repair services for homes in Minneapolis, Chicago, and Miami to gather data to train AI models and robots.
paragraph1: An AI lab that specializes in gathering real-world data wants to partner with homeowners to record how skilled laborers do their jobs to train AI robots.
paragraph2: HUMXN said it will subsidize plumbing, electrical, HVAC, air-duct cleaning, and carpet cleaning, allowing people who need these services to get them for free in exchange for letting someone in with “wearable capture technology” work inside their home.

author: TechPulse
excerpt: The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as…
paragraph1: The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26. Of the 102 startups in the tracker, 65, or about 63.7%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 65 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,511.8 Cr, while the remaining 37 posted a cumulative loss of ₹30,950.8 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem. Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 102 companies generated ₹4.75 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 34.62% increase from ₹3.53 Lakh Cr in FY25. To help you track the financial health of new-age tech companies, Inc42 has launched the FY26 Financial Tracker, bringing together key financial metrics in one place. The tracker will be updated periodically with the latest financial disclosures and deeper insights into the performance of India’s startup ecosystem. title: Top Stories: Apple HomeView, New Apple TV and HomePod mini, and Sold-Out iPhone Duo
title_bn: Top Stories: Apple HomeView, New Apple TV and HomePod mini, and Sold-Out iPhone Duo
author: TechPulse
excerpt: It was another crazy busy week for Apple, headlined by Tuesday seeing the company take the wraps off of several home-related products as part of a "Welcome home" launch wave. And as if that wasn't enough, Friday saw the start of iPhone Duo pre-orders
paragraph1: It was another crazy busy week for Apple, headlined by Tuesday seeing the company take the wraps off of several home-related products as part of a "Welcome home" launch wave. And as if that wasn't enough, Friday saw the start of iPhone Duo pre-orders with delivery estimates quickly slipping by months amid its popularity and apparent product shortages, while we're looking forward to even more products launches later this month, so read on below for all of the details! Top Stories Apple Announces 'HomeView' Smart Home Hub Apple's long-rumored smart home hub is finally official, with Apple debuting the $299 HomeView as part of its "Welcome home" product launch this week. Apple HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and Siri AI support, and it's available in both tabletop and wall mounted versions. The device is able to recognize multiple users and adjust its presentation of information depending on how far the user is from the screen, and it supports Photos faces, Apple Music playlists, FaceTime calls, and more. Pre-orders are underway now with a launch coming on November 13. New Apple TV 4K Announced With A19 Chip, Updated Siri Remote, More While the Apple HomeView was the headline attraction of this week's introductions, the Apple TV box also got its first update in four years with the unveiling of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
paragraph2: The new box gets a big upgrade to the A19 chip, which provides Siri AI support and improved performance. A new Siri Remote (also available separately for older boxes) includes Find My support with Precision Finding and a speaker to allow it to make itself heard when lost. And for times when you want to use Siri without the remote, the box itself also now includes microphones for hands-free Siri AI. The new box comes with a significant price hike to $299, and it's available for pre-order now ahead of a November 13 launch. Apple Announces $149 HomePod Mini 2 With Siri AI, 'Sound Glow', and Four-Speaker Surround Sound Apple's third home-related product announcement for the week was a new HomePod mini equipped with Siri AI, new colors, and improved audio experiences. The ‌HomePod‌ mini 2 has an S10 chip that supports advanced computational audio, and Apple says it optimizes dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance in real-time. A Sound Glow feature turns the ‌HomePod‌ mini's top into a "visual canvas" that glows and animates in sync with music, reacting to bass and treble.
paragraph3: It uses colors generated from the song's album artwork for a unique experience for each song. The HomePod mini 2 is priced at $149 and is available for pre-order now ahead of an October 30 launch. Siri AI won't be available at launch, however, as it will come in a future software update. iPhone Duo is Sold Out for Christmas as Shipping Estimates Slip to 2027 Apple began accepting iPhone Duo pre-orders in a number of countries at 5 a.m. Pacific Time on Friday, with delivery estimates starting to slip within minutes if not seconds. Within half an hour, delivery estimates in the U.
paragraph4: S. ultimately stabilized at late January 2027, a three-month delay. In remains to be seen how much, if any, stock Apple will have at its retail stores for walk-in purchases on the October 23 launch date, and scalpers are already selling off early pre-orders for as much as $5,000. Apple Inviting Media to October 28 'Launch Experience' After previously reporting that Apple was planning a two-day product showcase in Los Angeles on October 27 and 28 for select content creators and members of the media to experience even more upcoming Apple products, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman now says Apple has begun explicitly inviting members of the media to the event for October 28. We're expecting to see several more products launch on either October 27 or 28, including new high-end 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook models with touchscreen OLED displays, new iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro models based around the M6 chip, and a new iPad mini with an OLED display. MacRumors Newsletter Each week, we publish an email newsletter like this highlighting the top Apple stories, making it a great way to get a bite-sized recap of the week hitting all of the major topics we've covered and tying together related stories for a big-picture view. So if you want to have top stories like the above recap delivered to your email inbox each week, subscribe to our newsletter!

And as if that wasn't enough, Friday saw the start of iPhone Duo pre-orders with delivery estimates quickly slipping by months amid its popularity and apparent product shortages, while we're looking forward to even more products launches later this month, so read on below for all of the details! Top Stories Apple Announces 'HomeView' Smart Home Hub Apple's long-rumored smart home hub is finally official, with Apple debuting the $299 HomeView as part of its "Welcome home" product launch this week. Apple HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and Siri AI support, and it's available in both tabletop and wall mounted versions. The device is able to recognize multiple users and adjust its presentation of information depending on how far the user is from the screen, and it supports Photos faces, Apple Music playlists, FaceTime calls, and more. Pre-orders are underway now with a launch coming on November 13. New Apple TV 4K Announced With A19 Chip, Updated Siri Remote, More While the Apple HomeView was the headline attraction of this week's introductions, the Apple TV box also got its first update in four years with the unveiling of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
bangla_paragraph2: The new box gets a big upgrade to the A19 chip, which provides Siri AI support and improved performance. A new Siri Remote (also available separately for older boxes) includes Find My support with Precision Finding and a speaker to allow it to make itself heard when lost. And for times when you want to use Siri without the remote, the box itself also now includes microphones for hands-free Siri AI. The new box comes with a significant price hike to $299, and it's available for pre-order now ahead of a November 13 launch. Apple Announces $149 HomePod Mini 2 With Siri AI, 'Sound Glow', and Four-Speaker Surround Sound Apple's third home-related product announcement for the week was a new HomePod mini equipped with Siri AI, new colors, and improved audio experiences. The ‌HomePod‌ mini 2 has an S10 chip that supports advanced computational audio, and Apple says it optimizes dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance in real-time. A Sound Glow feature turns the ‌HomePod‌ mini's top into a "visual canvas" that glows and animates in sync with music, reacting to bass and treble.

The HomePod mini 2 is priced at $149 and is available for pre-order now ahead of an October 30 launch. title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
title_bn: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. Bu
paragraph1: Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web.
paragraph2: At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systemsThis ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well.
paragraph3: xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.
paragraph4: ” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors.
paragraph5: After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

title: Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
title_bn: Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
author: TechPulse
excerpt: After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of d
paragraph1: After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of decline.Part of the resurgence can be tied to the fact that they’re cool now with younger generations — following the revival of tape decks and vinyl. Celebrities have been spotted wearing them, and there’s even an Instagram account that follows the trend. Wired earbuds have real benefits. They don’t need a battery, so they’ll last longer than wireless ones that eventually die, and it’s a lot harder to lose a wired pair with a long cable than a single earbud.Now, after more than a decade, Bose has returned to the wired world, but the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are no throwbacks.8Verge Score$99The GoodOne of the few sets of wired earbuds with ANCComfortable and secure fitHigh-res audioSimple to useThe BadCall quality isn’t greatWind noise is distractingThe $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect over USB-C, so they don’t need an extra dongle to work with current phones. That’s also how they can offer ANC. Because the 3.5mm or 4.
paragraph2: 4mm analog audio connector doesn’t provide enough power for active noise cancellation, most wired earbuds, from cheap off-brands to wildly expensive audiophile in-ear monitors, rely on passive isolation only. Bose’s last attempt at wired in-ears with ANC, 2013’s QuietComfort 20, had a 3.5mm jack, and their ANC relied on a rechargeable battery in the cable. The new Bose earbuds don’t need the battery pack; they can get the minimal power they need for ANC from the USB-C port.There are a few other USB-C wired headphones with active noise cancellation, but not many. There’s also the $30 Belkin SoundForm ANC Wired Earbuds, which reportedly have weak noise canceling, and Audio-Technica released a pair in Asia earlier this year.The best part of the Bose earbuds, or any wired earbuds, is that they’re simple. No need to worry about pairing them, no need to charge them, and no need to fiddle with an app. Plug them into the USB-C port on a phone or computer and they just work.The in-line remote is super basic in the best way.While the noise canceling performance doesn’t measure up to Bose’s Bluetooth earbuds (the wired earbuds have two mics per side, while the QuietComfort Earbuds have three), it’s still solid for the price.
paragraph3: It does a great job blocking low-frequency sounds like air conditioners and low truck rumbles, but has difficulty muting conversation (with ANC on, I can’t hear our air conditioner at all, but can make out every word of my wife’s phone conversation as I write this). There’s a slight high-end hiss when the noise canceling is active, but it’s only noticeable when they aren’t playing any sound.And they sound great. Vocals are clear and bright, and bass is punchy without overwhelming other instruments. I wouldn’t mind being able to cut down the high-end brightness a bit (mainly to tame cymbal ringing), but since these don’t use an app there are no EQ options. The wired connection allows for low latency, so there’s no worry about sound and video lining up, and they support high-res audio at 24-bit/48kHz. I went back and forth between CD quality (16-bit/44.1kHz) and high-res streams of the new release of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul on Qobuz, and the high-res versions sounded a bit more open and spacious. It’s not an enormous difference, but I’d listen to the high-res version on the Bose over the CD-level stream any day.The in-line remote has three buttons that control volume, playback, and noise-canceling mode selection. They respond quickly when pressed and have a nice rubberized texture.
paragraph4: The headphones come with three ear tip sizes and two sets of wings to find a good fit (you don’t even need to use the wings if you find them uncomfortable). I was easily able to find a comfortable combination and they stayed securely in my ears for hours. The earbuds are also IPX4 rated if there’s a light rain while you’re out or you want to use them on a run.Even with the benefits of wired earbuds, though, nostalgia can’t wipe away the frustrations. If you don’t run the 4.2-foot cable under your shirt, or coil up the excess in your jacket pocket, it catches on everything. In my short time with the Bose, the cable caught on the handle of a kitchen drawer, the edge of my keyboard, the zipper of my sweatshirt, the strap of a bag I was carrying, my pocket (when I accidentally stuffed too much of the excess in with my phone), and even the hand of a stranger who got too close to me in line at Starbucks.There are three ear tip sizes and two wings available to find the right fit.And as with any wired earbuds, there’s cable noise, as vibrations from rubbing or bumping against something travel up the cable to be heard in the earbuds. Although I will say the cable insulation is enough to minimize the effect better than cheap (and older) options.The Bose struggle with wind.
paragraph5: The microphones for noise canceling or transparency mode pick up the wind noise, and it’s distracting — with ANC on, it cuts out the low-end whoosh decently, but the high end is still incredibly present. I found turning it off was best when it was windy outside, although that meant compromising on the noise canceling.Call quality also isn’t the best. The microphone is on the in-line remote, and it picks up a good amount of ambient sound during calls. If you regularly make calls while walking busy streets, these aren’t the earbuds for you.I’m not ready to go back to 2016 and convert back to wired earbuds. In most situations, the benefits of wireless earbuds outweigh those of wired ones, and I don’t see that changing for me. But for the ease of use, convenience of a USB-C connection, lack of lag, high-res capability, sound quality, and the fact they include ANC, the Bose are unquestionably the best affordable wired option out there.Photography by John Higgins / The VergeFollow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

title: Leap seconds being retired next year to avoid wreaking havoc on computer systems
title_bn: Leap seconds being retired next year to avoid wreaking havoc on computer systems
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The leap second will be replaced by a leap hour, which will take "several centuries" before it must be implemented.
paragraph1: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), which maintains the International System of Units (SI), has voted to expedite the retirement of the leap second, moving forward the date from 2035 to May 20, 2027, an adjustment that could wreak havoc on computer systems, which expect a consistent 60 seconds every minute.
paragraph2: The leap second is occasionally added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to ensure that it remains in-sync with the Earth’s rotation.
paragraph3: Our planet’s movement isn’t a constant one revolution every 24 hours owing to forces applied by the atmosphere, the oceans, its core, and even the Moon, and according to BIPM [PDF], these changes mean a 30% probability of needing a “negative leap second” by 2035.

Founded in 2006 by Hrush Bhatt, Matthew Spacie and Stuart Crighton, Cleartrip enables users to book flights, hotels, trains, buses and local activities through its website and app. Ecommerce major Flipkart acquired the company in 2021. In its financial statements, the company said its ability to continue as a going concern depended on the success of its operations and its ability to secure funding. However, it added that its holding company, Flipkart Internet Private Limited, had provided a commitment and letter of financial support. During FY26, Cleartrip borrowed ₹3,964 Cr from Flipkart Internet and repaid ₹3,653 Cr. Interest on these loans stood at ₹130.4 Cr for the year. The widening loss comes as Cleartrip seeks to reduce its reliance on discounts and diversify beyond flight bookings. In July 2026, the company said it was targeting operational break-even by the end of FY27. Its plans include growing its hotels, trains and buses businesses and increasing revenue from ancillary services. The company has also seen leadership changes in recent years.

title: Crafty OpenAI agent willingly stole crypto from an account it didn't own to complete a task during test
title_bn: Crafty OpenAI agent willingly stole crypto from an account it didn't own to complete a task during test
author: TechPulse
excerpt: GPT5.6-Sol didn't have funds to deploy smart contracts, so it looked for exposed accounts with enough money to pay for the gas fees.
paragraph1: OpenAI recently released a misalignment report on its GPT5.6-Sol coding agent after it stole cryptocurrency from an account it didn’t own.
paragraph2: It didn’t have enough funds for the smart contracts needed to execute its tasks, so it wrote a script that looked for accounts with public seed phrases that had enough funds to pay the gas fees, finished its task, and didn’t report that it took funds from an account it wasn’t assigned to without authorization.Thankfully, this all happened on the Sepolia test network, which uses Sepolia ETH, simulated ETH in a simulated Ethereum network for cryptocurrency app development; it doesn’t actually have any monetary value.
paragraph3: The report states, “The assignment asked it to update the trading calculator and database behavior, and to replace placeholder contract addresses with working deployments on Sepolia.” The final task required the agent to deploy smart contracts, a task that required gas fees paid in Sepolia ETH.
paragraph4: It wasn’t supplied with a funded wallet, nor was it permitted to use funds from another account it found.Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
title_bn: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
author: TechPulse
excerpt: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it's a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple's new smart
paragraph1: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious.There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.
paragraph2: ”The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook.“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll.
paragraph3: So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”— Jaya SaxenaIt’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance.
paragraph4: Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.”Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same.
paragraph5: For them, the choice remains as it has for some time: Stick it out with ever-diminishing Google traffic and ad revenue; take on more sponsored content and paid-for recipes with big brands; or move to a paywall or newsletter business model.Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.Some version of paid-for content may be the only answer going forward, though, for creators both big and small. Tech companies like Apple will have to grapple with how their tools work when access to free content gets trickier, and the rest of us may have to get used to paying for recipes again.“A good, creative recipe that has been tested to ensure it really works takes time and effort and money,” Saxena says. “It is a real skill to communicate how something is made when you’re not physically with that person, and buying all the ingredients needed to test things multiple times is expensive. People should probably be more comfortable paying for that.

title: It’s a dream week for tech docs
title_bn: It’s a dream week for tech docs
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 148, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you're new here, welcome, hope you're enjoying all your pumpkin-flavored everything, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer
paragraph1: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 148, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, hope you’re enjoying all your pumpkin-flavored everything, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)This week, I’ve been reading about Marc Andreessen and the future of math and Mike Tomlin and Citizens United, reminiscing about the heyday of MySpace, sending this article to everyone as an apology for my bad texting, listening to the Pet Shop Boys’ new Alan Turing album and Dwarkesh Patel’s thoughts on AI, barely keeping myself from preordering an iPhone Duo, asking a lot of questions about that “flying” Tesla Roadster, and endlessly shopping for tripods to hold my phone for social videos. I have thought way too much about tripods this week.I also have for you a couple of huge new tech docs and a whole bunch of gadgets worth a look. Gadget season, baby! Let’s go.(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / throwing in the trunk this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)The DropYou Can See Everything. I can’t remember the last time I was so excited about a documentary (especially a three-hour one). The pairing of Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder, the shocking level of access, the incredible meta-ness of the whole project. I’ll be seeing this the first minute I can.
paragraph2: Oh, and after you watch the doc, watch Josh Johnson’s hourlong set on all things Elizabeth Holmes. Glorious.Musk. And here’s four more hours of tech doc! The reviews here are also spectacular, and even if you’ve been following the news the last decade or so, I suspect seeing it all in a row at once is going to be an experience.The Apple HomeView. I keep staring at the buy button on this new $299 home hub. I’m not sure what I need it for, really — my very basic smart home is working just fine — but there’s something almost old-school about the idea of this as a sort of family computer. I’m certainly in the market for fewer reasons to look at my phone.The new Siri Remote. I cannot in good conscience recommend a $300 Apple TV, but I can totally tell you to drop $60 on the new Find My-enabled remote! I mean, wait until you lose your existing one first. But you will. These remotes are impossible.The Fairphone Fairbuds 2. I’ve come to like both Fairphone’s minimalist aesthetic and its emphasis on repairability, and the fact that it gets both into a lighter, smaller, longer-lasting, cheaper-than-AirPods package is pretty exciting.The Xbox Nano Controller. Look at this little guy!
paragraph3: A pocket-sized game controller comes in handy more often than you think (makes the waiting room a lot more fun), and this one has all the buttons you’d expect for Xbox and other games. If the battery life is good, this one’s gonna be a winner.The Fitbit Edge. I’ve been using a Fitbit Air for a while, and I like it a lot, but I do miss having a fitness tracker that also told me the time. This one does that, plus a little more workout and biometric tracking. It’s not the handsomest wristwear I’ve ever seen, but it is very Fitbit.The CMF Speaker S. I am a sucker for a cool Bluetooth speaker, and these futuristic milk carton-looking devices are fabulous. I bought one of the small ones immediately, and I’m already debating a second to build out the stereo pair. More companies should make speakers that look good!E Ink Kaleido 4. This isn’t so much a specific gadget as it is good news for a whole category of gadgets: We have a new version of the color E Ink panel found in lots of devices, with promises of both better colors and better performance. title: Game decompilation hub freezes leaderboard after AI turns progress into a hollow numbers game amid explosion of 'AI slop'
title_bn: Game decompilation hub freezes leaderboard after AI turns progress into a hollow numbers game amid explosion of 'AI slop'
author: TechPulse
excerpt: decomp.dev has closed its public index of game decompilation projects, saying AI-driven forks and ports broke the community.
paragraph1: The decomp.dev community that tracks and centralizes game decompilation progress is shutting down its public index and leaderboard, claiming in a site update that the acceleration of AI has damaged the decompilation community.
paragraph2: The creator, who goes by @encounter, points to abuses related to AI usage, such as AI helping forks “finish” others’ projects and a general attitude of rushing to complete PC ports, often with little regard to quality. Simply banning AI-assisted projects is a difficult task, as not all of them have the same standards, and @encounter feels it shouldn’t be the role of one hobbyist to decide what does and doesn’t stay on the leaderboard.
paragraph3: The decision was made because AI greatly speeds up decompilation “in a significant way,” especially with human guidance, but misuse of the technology has broken the community aspect. AI has made the progress percentages on decomp.
paragraph4: dev easier to push up. As a result, the site’s index and leaderboard are now “causing more harm than good,” as the competitive spirit has been corrupted.
paragraph5: The scene has become “a hollow numbers game” where people throw AI usage at things “to make number go up.”Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

title: Flipkart’s Logistics Arm Ekart Cuts FY26 Loss By 98% To ₹26 Cr
title_bn: Flipkart’s Logistics Arm Ekart Cuts FY26 Loss By 98% To ₹26 Cr
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26). Its…
paragraph1: SUMMARYInstakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26) Ekart’s total expenses for the fiscal dipped by 13% YoY to ₹13,638 Cr in the year under review, while its costs stood at ₹15,673 Cr in FY25 The brand’s revenue from contracts with customers fell 4.2% to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26, from ₹13,779 Cr in the previous fiscal year Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26). Its loss narrowed 98.3% to ₹26 Cr in the fiscal under review, compared to ₹1,508 Cr in FY25. The brand’s revenue from contracts with customers fell 4.2% to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26, from ₹13,779 Cr in the previous fiscal year.
paragraph2: In this, Flipkart itself contributed ₹9,112 Cr, or about 69% of the total operating revenue. Operationally, logistics, transportation and shipping contributed the most share, approximately 50% to ₹6,419 Cr in the reported year. Revenue from this vertical plunged 39.5% YoY. Ekart also generates revenue from collection services and warehousing services. Collection services income fell 68% to ₹510 Cr, while warehousing services income rose 44% to ₹2,212 Cr.
paragraph3: Including finance and other income of ₹418 Cr, Instakart’s total income fell 3.9% to ₹13,612 Cr in the year under review. Founded in 2009 by Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal as an in-house logistics entity within Flipkart, Ekart was spun off as a separate entity in 2016 to support the fulfillment services not only for Flipkart and Myntra but also for D2C brands, online sellers and retailers. As of last year, the company claimed to be operating more than 7,000 trucks running daily across the length and breadth of the country, 70 fulfilment centres, 80 sortation facilities and 3500 delivery hubs to ensure timely delivery across 14,000 pin codes. Earlier in July, Ekart opened its pan-India logistics network to MSMEs, D2C brands, FMCG companies, and enterprises, allowing external businesses to access the logistics infrastructure used by Flipkart. The logistics arm has already operationalised more than 300 franchise outlets across Surat, Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru, and had plans to expand the network to over 1,000 outlets by the end of 2026.
paragraph4: Magnifying Ekart’s Spending Ekart’s total expenses for the fiscal dipped by 13% YoY to ₹13,638 Cr in the year under review, while its costs stood at ₹15,673 Cr in FY25. Here is a closer look at where Ekart spent the highest: Freight, Handling and Servicing Expenses: The spending under this head fell by 17.1% to ₹9,191 Cr in FY25 from ₹11,093 Cr in the previous financial year. Of the overall expenditure, freight costs comprised 67.4%. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, which include salaries, provident fund, gratuity, among others, shrunk by 24.
paragraph5: 9% to ₹958 Cr from ₹1,275 Cr in FY25. Further, it accounted for 7% of the overall expenses in FY26. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: These costs increased by 5% to ₹1,456 Cr from ₹1,387 Cr in FY25.
